title: Drug use and dual diagnosis
blurb: Respond to opioid overdose, support people with psychosis who use drugs, and apply NICE's 'do not exclude' rules.
question: Dean, 29, has schizophrenia and uses heroin and cannabis. He is being discharged from the ward after 6 weeks without using. The community team has said it cannot take him 'until his drug use is sorted'. What should the ward nurse do?

teach.h: Dual diagnosis: two needs, one person
teach.body: Dual diagnosis means coexisting severe mental illness (such as psychosis or bipolar disorder) and substance misuse. NICE CG120 (healthcare settings) and NG58 (community health and social care) say mental health services take the lead, and that neither problem is a reason to shut the door on care for the other. Plain English: treat both, in the same plan, through the services the person already uses, without making them earn help by stopping first.

steps.label: Call 999
steps.sub: Or get someone else to call

teach.caption: Prenoxad SmPC (emc): repeat doses may be needed because some opioids last longer than naloxone. DHSC 2025: anyone can give available naloxone to save a life.

items.label: may give it in an emergency

teach.caption: Drug services, nurses, midwives, pharmacists, paramedics and others can supply naloxone without a prescription (DHSC, Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription, updated Sep 2025; Human Medicines Regulations as amended in 2024).

teach.body: After weeks of reduced or no use in hospital, prison or detox, the body's tolerance to opioids falls. Using the old dose can then cause a fatal overdose. CG120 1.6.6 says that on discharge people must be told about the risk of overdose if they start using again, especially opioids, and must have a care coordinator and a care plan covering both needs. Plain English: the safest moment to talk about overdose is before the door opens.

head: Do
Why
rows: Ask everyone with psychosis about alcohol and drugs
Assess drug users for possible psychosis
Agree any urine or blood tests first

items: Meet immediate needs wherever the person presents: housing, physical health, food (1.1.1, 1.1.4).
A care coordinator in community mental health services leads the care plan; review it at every contact (1.2.2, 1.2.5).
Do not discharge because of a missed appointment: treat non-attendance as a concern and follow it up (1.3.8, 1.6.5).
Adapt existing services rather than create a separate 'dual diagnosis' service (1.5.5).
Offer harm reduction alongside work on change and relapse prevention (1.5.6).

teach.body: The nurse challenges the refusal: NICE says people with psychosis must not be excluded from mental health care because of substance misuse. She asks for a named care coordinator and a care plan covering both his psychosis and drug use, links in substance misuse services, and explains to Dean that after 6 weeks without heroin his tolerance is low, so his old dose could kill him. She offers take-home naloxone and shows Dean and his sister how to use it.

teach.text: 'Sort the drugs first, then we'll treat the illness' is the classic error. NICE says do not exclude people with SMI from mental health services because of substance misuse, or from substance misuse services because of psychosis. Also, one dose of naloxone does not end the emergency: it can wear off before the opioid.

items: Do not exclude from mental health care, drug services, accommodation or contingency management because of the other condition.
Mental health services lead, with a care coordinator and one plan for both needs.
Opioid overdose: call 999, naloxone IM, repeat every 2-3 minutes as needed, stay, and get hospital observation.
Warn about lost tolerance at discharge; biological tests only by agreement, not routine screening.

summary: You can now respond to an opioid overdose with naloxone, knowing why it may need repeating, and warn people about lost tolerance. You can also apply NICE CG120 and NG58 so people with coexisting psychosis and substance misuse are assessed, treated and not excluded.

A.q: Why may a person given naloxone for a heroin overdose need further doses and hospital observation?
options: Naloxone causes rebound sedation after 20 minutes
Naloxone works for 1-2 hours; opioids can last longer
Naloxone reverses synthetic opioids but not heroin itself
Naloxone must be followed by intravenous flumazenil
A.why: The Prenoxad SmPC states naloxone's effect lasts 1-2 hours, shorter than most opioids, so repeat doses may be needed and the person should be observed.

whyNot.0: Naloxone does not cause rebound sedation; the opioid's effect returning is the danger.
whyNot.2: Naloxone reverses opioids including heroin, a natural opiate derivative.
whyNot.3: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and is not a routine follow-on.

A.q: According to NICE, which response to a person with schizophrenia who uses cannabis is correct?
options: Accept for mental health care and address both needs
Refer to drug services and close the mental health referral
Accept once three negative urine screens are recorded
Admit for planned detox before any assessment
A.why: CG120 1.4.3 and NG58 1.2.1: do not exclude people with psychosis or SMI from mental health care because of substance misuse; assess and treat both.

whyNot.1: Closing the referral excludes him because of substance misuse.
whyNot.2: Biological tests are not for routine screening or as an entry condition.
whyNot.3: Assessment comes first; detox is planned within the care plan.

A.q: A colleague wants to send routine urine drug screens for everyone on the early intervention caseload. What does NICE CG120 say?
options: Test everyone at each visit to detect hidden use
Test anyone who has missed an appointment
Test monthly as a condition of treatment
Agree tests with the person, not as routine screening
A.why: CG120 1.4.15: biological tests may help but should be agreed with the person as part of the care plan; do not use them for routine screening in psychosis.

whyNot.0: Routine screening is what CG120 advises against.
whyNot.1: Non-attendance calls for follow-up, not a drug test.
whyNot.2: Making tests a condition of treatment conflicts with the agreed, person-centred approach.

B.q: On a community visit, you find Kerry unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. After calling 999, what is the next action?
options: Give naloxone 400 micrograms IM
Give oral glucose gel between cheek and gum
Wait for paramedics before any drug is given
Give rescue breaths for 2 minutes, then reassess
B.why: Signs suggest opioid overdose: give naloxone (Prenoxad 0.4 mL, 400 micrograms IM), repeat every 2-3 minutes if needed, and stay with her, starting CPR if she stops breathing normally.

whyNot.1: Oral gel is unsafe in an unresponsive person and does not reverse opioids.
whyNot.2: Anyone may give available naloxone to save a life; waiting wastes time.
whyNot.3: Breaths support her but do not reverse the opioid; naloxone is given now.

B.q: Sam has bipolar disorder and uses cocaine. He has missed two appointments with the community team. What does NICE NG58 advise?
options: Discharge him to his GP after two missed visits
Treat non-attendance as a concern and follow up
Send a letter asking him to re-refer himself
Wait for him to contact the team when ready
B.why: NG58 1.3.8 and 1.6.5: do not discharge automatically for missed appointments; view non-attendance as a concern and follow up, for example by phone, home visit or contacting carers.

whyNot.0: Automatic discharge for non-attendance is what NG58 warns against.
whyNot.2: Putting the onus on him risks losing contact with a high-risk person.
whyNot.3: Passive waiting ignores that this group is at high risk of losing contact.

B.q: Tariq has psychosis and long-standing heroin dependence and wants a planned detoxification. Where does NICE CG120 advise this should happen?
options: At home with daily pharmacy pick-ups
In a police custody suite under supervision
In an inpatient setting with substance misuse advice
In a separate dual diagnosis unit
B.why: CG120 1.4.8 and 1.6.4: planned detox for people with psychosis should take place in an inpatient setting, preferably specialist detox units or designated beds, with substance misuse services involved.

whyNot.0: CG120 places planned detox in psychosis in an inpatient setting.
whyNot.1: Custody is not a treatment setting.
whyNot.3: NICE advises adapting existing services rather than creating a separate dual diagnosis service.

C.q: Ten minutes after naloxone, Kerry is awake, angry and wants to leave before the ambulance arrives. She says she feels fine. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Let her go, as the overdose is reversed
Explain naloxone may wear off and urge her to stay
Restrain her until the paramedics arrive
Give a second dose of naloxone before she leaves
C.why: Naloxone lasts about 1-2 hours, often shorter than the opioid, so she could slip back into overdose; explain this, encourage her to wait and keep her company, and hand over to paramedics.

whyNot.0: Waking up does not mean the opioid has gone.
whyNot.2: Restraint is not lawful or proportionate if she has capacity and chooses to leave.
whyNot.3: A further dose is given if breathing worsens, not routinely before she goes.

C.q: Dean is leaving the ward after 6 weeks without heroin. Which discharge plan meets NICE CG120?
options: Discharge with care led by the drug service
Discharge once he signs an abstinence agreement
Discharge with a 4-week supply of all his medicines
A care plan for both needs and an overdose warning
C.why: CG120 1.6.6: on discharge ensure an identified care coordinator, a care plan covering both psychosis and substance misuse, and information on overdose risk if he starts using again, especially opioids.

whyNot.0: Mental health services lead care for coexisting psychosis.
whyNot.1: Abstinence contracts are not a NICE discharge condition.
whyNot.2: Large supplies add overdose risk and do not meet the CG120 requirements.

C.q: Lena, 24, with bipolar disorder, has been offered a supported housing place. The provider withdraws it when she mentions she drinks alcohol most days. What does NICE say?
options: Accept it, as providers set their own rules
Ask her to complete a detox before reapplying
Seek a place in a hostel for drinkers instead
Do not exclude her from staffed housing for this alone
C.why: CG120 1.7.1: do not exclude people with psychosis and coexisting substance misuse from staffed accommodation solely because of their substance misuse; NG58 also says do not exclude from housing or support services.

whyNot.0: NICE expects services to adapt rather than exclude.
whyNot.1: Requiring detox first excludes her because of substance use.
whyNot.2: Diverting her ignores the assessed need for supported housing.

reteach.title: Include, protect, follow up
reteach.question: What three things does NICE ask of every service for dual diagnosis?

blocks.body: Include: do not exclude from mental health care, drug services or housing because of the other problem. Protect: warn about lost tolerance and give naloxone where opioids are used. Follow up: a missed appointment is a warning sign, not a reason to discharge.

blocks.text: Naloxone wakes the person, but the opioid may outlast it.

explain.body: No exclusion from mental health care because of substance misuse, from substance misuse services because of psychosis, from accommodation or from contingency management.

test.q: Which service decision is consistent with NICE CG120?
options: Drug service refuses a client because he hears voices
Ward discharges a patient for using cannabis on leave
Mental health team accepts a client who uses heroin
Hostel removes a resident with psychosis for drinking
test.why: CG120: do not exclude people with psychosis and coexisting substance misuse from mental health care because of their substance use.

whyNot.0: Drug services should not exclude people because of psychosis (1.4.4).
whyNot.1: Do not discharge solely because of substance misuse (1.6.5).
whyNot.3: Do not exclude from staffed accommodation solely for substance misuse (1.7.1).

explain.body: Call 999, give naloxone IM (Prenoxad 0.4 mL), repeat every 2-3 minutes as needed, stay with the person. Effect lasts 1-2 hours.

test.q: Who may give available naloxone to save a life in an opioid overdose emergency in the UK?
options: Doctors and paramedics with a prescription
Registered nurses on a patient group direction
Drug service staff trained in its use
Anyone who has it available
test.why: DHSC guidance (2025): anyone can use available naloxone to save a life in an emergency.

whyNot.0: No prescription is needed to give it in an emergency.
whyNot.1: Emergency use is not limited to nurses or PGDs.
whyNot.2: Drug service staff can supply it, but administration is not limited to them.

explain.body: Reduced use in hospital, prison or detox lowers tolerance; returning to the old dose risks overdose. Warn at discharge.

test.q: Why does NICE CG120 ask staff to warn people with psychosis about overdose at discharge from hospital?
options: Antipsychotics raise opioid levels in the blood
Their tolerance to opioids may have fallen
Street drugs are stronger after a hospital stay
Naloxone cannot be used after a hospital stay
test.why: CG120 1.6.6: tell people about the risk of overdose if they start reusing substances, especially opioids, that were reduced or stopped during the inpatient stay; tolerance will have fallen.

whyNot.0: The CG120 reason is reduced tolerance, not this interaction.
whyNot.2: Drug strength is not linked to the person's admission.
whyNot.3: Naloxone can be used at any time.

explain.body: Ask everyone with psychosis about substances; assess drug users for psychosis; low-level use matters; tests by agreement, not routine screening.

test.q: Rhys, 20, with first-episode psychosis, says he 'only' smokes a little cannabis at weekends. How should the nurse view this?
options: Low-level use can still worsen his psychosis
Weekend use is too little to affect psychosis
Address cannabis once his antipsychotic takes effect
Cannabis protects against relapse at low doses
test.why: CG120 1.4.13: low levels of substance use that would not usually be harmful can significantly affect the mental health of people with psychosis.

whyNot.1: CG120 warns that small amounts can matter in psychosis.
whyNot.2: Substance use should be assessed and addressed from the start.
whyNot.3: There is no protective effect; it can worsen psychosis.
